catalog_quote: 1.1. Non-Linear Phoneme is stress, which is of two kinds, normal and emphatic. Normal stress coincides with the utterances of one syllable in any given word: symbol ′. Phonetically, there are three levels of normal stress: heavy, intermediate, and light. Heavy stress occurs on one syllable of every free form; the other syllables have light stress: ǧós ‘deity’ [ˈˈdʒɔs]; píǧin ‘business’ [ˈˈpɪ-dʒɪn]; hwáfæšən ‘how’ [ˈˈhwa-fæ-ʃən]; bilóŋ ‘to be’ [bɪ-ˈˈlɔŋ]. Intermediate stress occurs in complementary distribution with heavy stress; a word used as the second member of a compound (§ 3) has intermediate stress on the syllable which, when the word is independent, has heavy stress: ǧós-píǧin ‘having-God-as-a-business (adj.)’ ... Emphatic stress involves extra force of air expended on the usually accented syllable ... and gives emphatic meaning to the word thus accented. Words combined in a phra…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage from Hall 1944 sec. 1.1 is verbatim on the held page images (JAOS 64.3 pp. 95-96) and in the held scanned; locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1944 structuralist grammar sketch, but it is the only first-hand phonological description of this extinct pidgin and every later treatment located (held APiCS survey; Shi 1991 abstract; Miron 2020 fetched sources now) either defers to Hall on stress or is silent; no instrumental or later prosodic study exists per Glottolog's list and web search. (3) The LEXICAL coding follows from Hall treating stress as a phoneme, marking one heavy stress per free form on every word with no positional or weight rule, and same-length words differing (píǧin vs bilóŋ); the A-reader's caveat that Hall's informants were English-speaking CPE users is already recorded in the notes and does not change the verdict. sources.note: Longest modern linguistic sketch (41 pp.) with a phonology section built from Chinese-character phrasebook sources; would show whether Chinese-speaker CPE prosody (vs Hall's English-speaker informants) is described at all. Abstract seen (Airiti record) says CPE 'drew largely upon the morphology and phonology of Cantonese'; stress content unverified.

sources.note: The APiCS survey we hold cites p. 89 of this paper for the only post-Hall observation on CPE prosody (character tones tracking stress, e.g. low tone on the unstressed second syllable of 'open'); reading it would let the tone_note rest on the primary rather than the survey's paraphrase. Does not bear on the LEXICAL verdict.
